segments.title: Opening of the Smithsonian interview
segments.summary: Brown introduces the Smithsonian NEA Jazz Master interview with Sheila Jordan in her New York apartment and asks for her birth details.

segments.title: Born in Detroit, raised by grandparents in a Pennsylvania mining town
segments.summary: Jordan explains her young mother, being raised by her grandparents in Summerhill, Pennsylvania, her return to Detroit and hearing Charlie Parker, and singing from age three despite a hard life near the mine explosions.

segments.title: Native American heritage, absent father, and the pull of Bird and alcohol
segments.summary: She explains the 'half-breed' teasing, her absent father, vowing to dedicate her life to Bird's music, and how club work in the Village led to her drinking.

segments.title: Parents, grandparents and coal-mining poverty
segments.summary: She names her parents and grandparents, describes mine explosions, her aunts and uncles raised like siblings, and her Cherokee/Six Nation heritage.

segments.title: Singing grandparents, the cruel piano teacher and being teased for singing
segments.summary: Her drinking grandparents sang, her great aunt Alma hit her knuckles during piano lessons, and schoolmates teased her until she stopped singing.

segments.title: Mr. Rushing brings her back to singing
segments.summary: A high school music teacher gets her to sing at a school event and the feeling returns; she reflects that poverty made her strong and she needed to find Bird's music.

segments.title: Finding the Club Sudan and meeting Skeeter Spight and Leroy Mitchell
segments.summary: In Detroit she finds the Club Sudan, meets Tommy, Barry, Kenny and the scat singers Skeeter Spight and Leroy Mitchell, and her friend Jackie Berkhoff.

segments.title: The vocal trio in Detroit and learning Bird's lines from 78s
segments.summary: They sing Bird lines and lyrics a cappella as a trio for years; she praises Skeeter's scatting and wears out Charlie Parker 78s learning the lines.

segments.title: What captivated her about hearing Charlie Parker
segments.summary: Four notes of Bird raised the hair on her arm and she dedicated her life to the music; Bird later became like a big brother.

segments.title: No formal musical training; grandmother's background
segments.summary: She had no training beyond Mr. Rushing and learned entirely by ear; her grandmother had been raised Catholic with piano training.

segments.title: Where she lived in Detroit
segments.summary: She locates her home near Woodward Avenue and John R, with Cameron Brown commenting as a fellow Detroiter.

segments.title: Racial prejudice in Detroit and the high school principal
segments.summary: She saw race riots, identified with her Black friends, and was told by her principal not to associate with 'colored girls'.

segments.title: Teen jobs, leaving her mother's home, the commercial course, and siblings
segments.summary: Police harassment, office work, her mother's many husbands, leaving home for a rooming house, her commercial diploma and her half-siblings.

segments.title: Hearing Charlie Parker at the Greystone Ballroom
segments.summary: Living in a rooming house, she and friends stand in front of Bird at the Greystone and recall his sidemen and her friendship with Roy Haynes.

segments.title: Sitting in at Detroit clubs and singing for John Lewis
segments.summary: She hung out at the Blue Bird Inn, was nicknamed Jeannie, and sang her Afternoon in Paris lyrics to John Lewis, who disliked the lyrics but liked her singing.

segments.title: Dancing the Bop to Bird and singing for Dizzy
segments.summary: Detroiters danced the Bop to Bird, and Billy Mitchell told visiting musicians about the trio, who sang for Bird and Dizzy.

segments.chapter: New York: Bird and the loft years
segments.title: Frank Foster, Bird at Birdland, and marrying Duke Jordan
segments.summary: She lived with Frank Foster in Detroit, introduced him to Bird at Birdland while he was on leave from the Korean War, and then married Bird's pianist Duke Jordan.

segments.chapter: New York: Bird and the loft years
segments.title: Moving to New York and supporting the music by typing
segments.summary: She moved on her own, relying on her commercial skills and typing for 58 years to 'support the music until it can support me'.

segments.chapter: New York: Bird and the loft years
segments.title: Cocktail Sips with Bird and his 'million dollar ears' remark
segments.summary: Bird had her sing at Cocktail Sips, told her she had million dollar ears and that if you can't say it in two choruses you never will; she explains she learned by ear.

segments.chapter: New York: Bird and the loft years
segments.title: Teaching jazz singing workshops at City College
segments.summary: John Lewis and Eddie Summerlin led her to start a workshop in 1978; she teaches learning the original melody and never breaking students' spirits.

segments.chapter: New York: Bird and the loft years
segments.title: Temp work, Brooklyn with Duke, and the 26th Street loft
segments.summary: She finds typing work, lives in Brooklyn with Duke, then takes half a loft near Eighth Avenue where all-night sessions happen and Bird sleeps on 'Bird's Bed'.

segments.chapter: New York: Bird and the loft years
segments.title: The parakeet that greeted Bird
segments.summary: Her talking parakeet Torrey says 'Hello, Bird' to the dozing Parker, who accuses her of ventriloquism; she regrets having no camera at the loft sessions.

segments.chapter: New York: Bird and the loft years
segments.title: Loft visitors, Mingus and Max send her to Tristano, Duke's decline, daughter Traci
segments.summary: Sonny and Monk visited the loft; Mingus and Max recommended Lennie Tristano; Duke drifted away and she took herself to the hospital when Traci was born in 1955.

segments.chapter: New York: Bird and the loft years
segments.title: Bird's addiction and his worry about the loft stairs
segments.summary: She describes Bird's addiction as a disease, his phone call to his mother, and how he cleared the loft of guests fearing the old floors would collapse.

segments.chapter: New York: Bird and the loft years
segments.title: Monk staring at the sky from the loft windows
segments.summary: Monk visits wordlessly and spends long stretches with his head out the tall window looking at the sky.

segments.chapter: New York: Bird and the loft years
segments.title: Learning how hard Monk's music is, and singing at his funeral
segments.summary: She first thought Monk's music simple, found it the hardest she had tried to sing, and later sang at his funeral at Barry Harris's request.

segments.chapter: New York: Bird and the loft years
segments.title: Monk falling off the stage at the Village Gate
segments.summary: She recalls seeing Monk dance and fall off the high stage at the Village Gate, then get back up and play.

segments.chapter: New York: Bird and the loft years
segments.title: Bird barred from Birdland
segments.summary: Bird, in a T-shirt, is refused entry to the club named after him, and she takes him to play slot machines instead.

segments.chapter: New York: Bird and the loft years
segments.title: Bird's cab ride, payment by check, and the 'messenger of the music'
segments.summary: She recounts accompanying Bird to feed his horse, his paying the cab with a check, his drinking troubles, and her view of Bird and herself as messengers of the music.

segments.title: Mingus never taught her; his tune Eclipse
segments.summary: She corrects her biography: Mingus took her to Tristano but never taught her, and he played Eclipse for her and later gave it to someone else.

segments.title: Horace Silver's piano, Tristano sessions and the bass-and-voice idea
segments.summary: She gave Horace Silver her old piano, started loft sessions after Tristano's, learned self-belief from Lennie, and developed bass and voice with Peter Ind.

segments.title: Mingus pushes her to sing in a Toledo club
segments.summary: Visiting her half-sister in Toledo, she is called up by Mingus with Lee Konitz and sings Yesterdays in her first club bass-and-voice performance.

segments.title: Lennie Tristano as a teacher
segments.summary: Tristano loved Bird, had her sing Parker solos, and taught her to ask pianists to play for her as for a horn player; as his first singer she got encouragement rather than theory.

segments.chapter: Prejudice, motherhood and the Page Three
segments.title: Dating the loft years, losing the loft after Traci, John Hendricks on the bus
segments.summary: Around 1952 she ran loft sessions; after Traci was born the landlord made her move, and she once heard John Hendricks singing on a bus.

segments.chapter: Prejudice, motherhood and the Page Three
segments.title: Arrested at Belle Isle for being in an interracial group
segments.summary: With Frank, Jenny King and Gunther she is stopped on the way to a picnic, taken to the police station and threatened by a detective, which convinces her to leave Detroit for New York.

segments.chapter: Prejudice, motherhood and the Page Three
segments.title: Rescued from a beating in New York; reflections on American racism
segments.summary: A plainclothesman with a gun stops white men attacking her and two Black painters; she and Brown reflect on racism and the election of a biracial president.

segments.chapter: Prejudice, motherhood and the Page Three
segments.title: Working as a typist, Traci's birth and Duke leaving
segments.summary: After Tristano she works in an office and sings a few nights a week; daughter Traci Jerrell Jordan is born and Duke gradually disappears.

segments.chapter: Prejudice, motherhood and the Page Three
segments.title: Hymie's apartment and Detroit musicians staying; Elvin Jones as baby-sitter
segments.summary: Landlord Herman finds her a place on 26th Street; Detroit musicians stay at her loft and Elvin Jones briefly baby-sits Traci.

segments.chapter: Prejudice, motherhood and the Page Three
segments.title: Singing at the Page Three and Herbie Nichols
segments.summary: At the Page Three club on Seventh Avenue, Herbie Nichols accompanies her and takes her on an out-of-body musical trip with Lilac Wine and Love for Sale.

segments.chapter: Prejudice, motherhood and the Page Three
segments.title: George Russell hears her and records her singing You Are My Sunshine
segments.summary: George Russell hears her at the Page Three, visits her grandmother's Pennsylvania mining club with her, and has her sing You Are My Sunshine on his Outer View record, her first professional recording.

segments.chapter: Prejudice, motherhood and the Page Three
segments.title: George Russell's tape leads to the Blue Note record
segments.summary: Russell shops her tape to Blue Note and Mercury; Blue Note signs her, with Quincy Jones's later letter, and she gets guitar, Denzil Best and Steve Swallow.

segments.chapter: Portrait of Sheila and jingle work
segments.title: Session personnel and recording George Russell's Outer View track
segments.summary: She names the players on the George Russell date including Paul Plummer, recalls rehearsing and recording quickly, and discusses the quiet second chorus.

segments.chapter: Portrait of Sheila and jingle work
segments.title: Recording Portrait of Sheila at Van Gelder's; Denzil Best
segments.summary: On her first record under her name, engineer Rudy Van Gelder is strict and Denzil Best tells Russell she scares him because he never knows if she will make it.

segments.chapter: Portrait of Sheila and jingle work
segments.title: Singing the record during an ectopic pregnancy
segments.summary: She was seriously ill with an undiagnosed ectopic pregnancy during the session, with Steve Swallow and Barry Galbraith supportive.

segments.chapter: Portrait of Sheila and jingle work
segments.title: Guitar, bass and drums instead of bass and voice
segments.summary: She wanted bass and voice but the producers refused, so Russell's guitar, bass and drums idea won; she had not sung with guitar before.

segments.chapter: Portrait of Sheila and jingle work
segments.title: Choosing the repertoire from her Page Three sets
segments.summary: She chose all the tunes herself, songs she had been trying out at the Page Three.

segments.chapter: Portrait of Sheila and jingle work
segments.title: No touring after the record; jingles for an advertising agency
segments.summary: The record led to little beyond a Vanguard week; her agency job led to jazz-sound jingles for Whirlpool, Bulova and others, with residual checks.

segments.chapter: Portrait of Sheila and jingle work
segments.title: Tape change
segments.summary: The tape is changed.

segments.chapter: Europe and a single mother's career
segments.title: Performing with George Russell at Newport and later
segments.summary: She appeared with Russell's sextet at Newport in 1964, at the Modern Museum of Art and later in Boston, usually only to sing Sunshine.

segments.chapter: Europe and a single mother's career
segments.title: The Page Three closes; raising Traci alone
segments.summary: The gay club Page Three was closed down; she kept her day job at the agency and raised her daughter alone.

segments.chapter: Europe and a single mother's career
segments.title: First trip to Europe via George Russell
segments.summary: Russell got her a gig at Ronnie Scott's and a Stockholm festival; she took Traci, felt embraced in Europe, and won the Down Beat critics award nine times.

segments.chapter: Europe and a single mother's career
segments.title: Why she never had an agent
segments.summary: She was shy and afraid of leaving her daughter, got gigs through musicians' calls and Russell, and always found places to sing.

segments.title: The Jazz in July workshop
segments.summary: Thanks to Max Roach and Fred Tillis she began teaching vocalists at Jazz in July after a year's delay, since the earlier teacher was a spirit breaker.

segments.title: Putney and Woodstock workshops with Attila Zoller, Jay Clayton and Fred Haas
segments.summary: She tells how Attila Zoller's instrumental workshop in Putney added singers, how Jay Clayton joined her, a Vermont vocal workshop, and a trip to Crete with Cameron Brown.

segments.title: How she runs a vocal workshop
segments.summary: She opens with a blues where each student sings their name and why they want to sing, teaches bebop lines and repertoire, and works individually in front of the group.

segments.title: The 'scat virus' and learning the original melody
segments.summary: She tells students they can be jazz singers without scatting, prescribes bebop lines as the cure, and says to learn the original melody first.

segments.title: The joy of teaching and nurturing a group
segments.summary: Teaching gives her the same thrill as performing, though she avoids teaching on a performance day; Brown praises her mix of group and individual work.

segments.title: Pitch problems, lead sheets and how to talk down a tune
segments.summary: She sends pitch problems to voice teachers, teaches students gently, and shows how to count intros, endings and keys using charts copied by Cameron Brown.

segments.title: Composer names on charts and the music lost in a taxi
segments.summary: She explains why charts list composers, recalls leaving all her originals in a cab on the way to a gig with Roswell Rudd, and where she met Cameron Brown.

segments.title: Abbey Lincoln and Billie Holiday as non-scat singers
segments.summary: She mentions Abbey Lincoln and a lost tape of Billie Holiday scatting at a party as examples that singers needn't scat.

segments.title: Hunting for lost tapes and loft photographs
segments.summary: Brown suggests asking jazz historians about the tape, and she wishes she could identify photographers from her late-1940s and early-1950s loft days.

segments.title: Moving between styles: melody before lyrics
segments.summary: Asked about working from bebop to George Russell and Roswell Rudd, she says she does not think in styles and chooses songs for their melody rather than lyrics.

segments.title: Billie Holiday and Lady in Satin
segments.summary: She loves Lady in Satin, hears Billie as a subtle improviser whose whole life comes through, and defends her late voice as a parting gift.

segments.title: Ella Fitzgerald, Sarah Vaughan and hearing Lady Be Good
segments.summary: Nobody sang like Billie and nobody but Skeeter scatted like Ella; hearing Ella's Lady Be Good on the Detroit radio turned her on to scatting.

segments.title: What became of Skeeter, Mitch and Willie
segments.summary: Skeeter died working with troubled kids, Mitch went blind, and Willie and a few others survive; Frank Foster has just died.

segments.title: Sobriety and the spiritual awakening
segments.summary: After eight years off alcohol and a stint with cocaine, a spiritual voice warns her that her gift will be taken away, and she joins AA, which she credits with saving her life.

segments.title: Roswell Rudd and trombone-and-voice
segments.summary: She describes Rudd, who suggested trombone and voice, as a gentle musician who plays bebop, Dixieland and free music, and recalls his tune from taxicab sounds.

segments.title: Don Cherry, George Gruntz's jazz operas and the lyrics to Art Deco
segments.summary: She recalls meeting Don Cherry, performing in Gruntz's jazz operas Money and Cosmopolitan Greetings, and writing words to Cherry's Art Deco after his death as Art of Don.

segments.title: Recording on ECM with Steve Kuhn and Steve Swallow
segments.summary: She recounts recording with Steve Kuhn's group and on Swallow's Robert Creeley setting Home.

segments.title: Steve Kuhn's group and the bass-and-voice duo with Harvey S.
segments.summary: Joining Kuhn's group with Bob Moses and Harvey Swartz led to years of bass-and-voice work with Harvey until he left, when she turned to Cameron Brown.

segments.title: Bass-and-voice programs with Cameron Brown
segments.summary: She explains the fifty-year-old bass-and-voice dream and the dedication programs she and Cameron perform for Bird, Prez and Billy, Miles, Ellington and others.

segments.chapter: Fire, film, NEA award and Billy Taylor
segments.title: The house fire and the rose that bloomed in the ashes
segments.summary: Her upstate house, bought with earnings from Gruntz's operas, burned while she was touring; she kept working, and a rose bloom and an unburned sympathy card told her everything would be all right.

segments.chapter: Fire, film, NEA award and Billy Taylor
segments.title: The documentary In the Voice of a Woman
segments.summary: Cade Bursell heard her sing and made a self-funded documentary, filming the Pennsylvania mines and the Green Mill and ending with her song The Crossing about sobriety.

segments.chapter: Fire, film, NEA award and Billy Taylor
segments.title: Learning she had been named an NEA Jazz Master
segments.summary: After a Toronto teaching trip, the NEA's Wayne Brown phones to announce the award, she mistakes him for a telemarketer, and she says she is in shock and only wants to keep the music alive.

segments.chapter: Fire, film, NEA award and Billy Taylor
segments.title: Tape change and start of the second session with Cameron Brown
segments.summary: The tape changes and Brown announces the continuation of the interview with bassist Cameron Brown joining.

segments.chapter: Fire, film, NEA award and Billy Taylor
segments.title: Billy Taylor, from Minton's After Hours to advocacy
segments.summary: She remembers first seeing a well-dressed Billy Taylor sit in at Minton's after hours, and credits him with promoting her and getting jazz into the mainstream.

segments.title: How the Jordan-Brown duo began, the Belgian concert and first record
segments.summary: Cameron Brown recalls rehearsing with her weekly for a Belgian project with Dave Ballou and Dewey Redman, then recording their first duo concert in Belgium, later released by Joe Fields.

segments.title: Duo repertoire and medleys
segments.summary: Cameron describes her ideas for medleys such as Blue Skies with a modulating bridge, and new numbers like Wouldn't It Be Loverly.

segments.title: Bird-and-Fats medley with Bird's intro to Scrapple
segments.summary: They build medleys like the dance songs and a Bird and Fats Waller medley, with Cameron's idea of using Bird's Scrapple intro under Honeysuckle Rose.

segments.title: Free improvisation and the Billy and Prez medley
segments.summary: The duo mixes open Native American-style improvisation, her song about musicians, and a Billie and Prez medley opening with Mingus's Goodbye Pork Pie Hat.

segments.title: Trust and spontaneity in the duo
segments.summary: She tells Cameron not to be shocked when she changes things; he describes letting go of responsibility and trusting her and the repertoire more as the partnership matured.

segments.title: Letting failure show: the throat that went out during Confirmation
segments.summary: She describes admitting when an idea fails, and singing 'Where were you?' to her returning voice over the changes of Confirmation at Vitello's, which relaxed the audience.

segments.title: Upcoming and recent gigs
segments.summary: They mention a Woodstock concert, the New York Society Library date and a festival in Crete.

segments.title: Being laid off at 58 and singing full-time
segments.summary: Laid off from the advertising agency at 58 with a year's severance, she went out as a singer, prayed for more singing, and has worked more ever since.

segments.title: Respect and no egos with Cameron
segments.summary: She calls Cameron a kid brother and a kindred spirit with no ego about billing.

segments.title: Cameron on the challenge of bass and voice and playing out of silence
segments.summary: Cameron says the duo is naked and challenging, grounded in silence as Miles understood; she is grateful for their partnership and his encouragement to write lyrics.

segments.title: Writing lyrics for Don Cherry's Remembrance
segments.summary: Rediscovering the heavy lyrics she wrote, she doubts she wrote them.

segments.title: Lyrics for Dannie Richmond's Soft Seas
segments.summary: At Cameron's urging she writes words for Dannie Richmond's calypso Soft Seas, picturing him going home to be buried.

segments.title: How she came to write lyrics; asking the composer's permission
segments.summary: On the Belgian project she insisted on lyrics, wrote Art of Don only after Cherry's death, says she is not a composer, and notes lyrics need the composer's permission.

segments.title: Cameron's years with Dannie Richmond's group after Mingus
segments.summary: Brown notes Cameron played with George Adams, Don Pullen and Dannie Richmond for eight and a half years after Mingus's death, and Cameron wrote a lullaby for them.

segments.title: Being hard on herself and never listening back
segments.summary: She always thinks she could do better and still can't bear to hear her recordings.

segments.title: Working in Cameron's Here and Now band and with Don Byron
segments.summary: She came to enjoy Cameron's Here and Now band despite its outness, toured Europe with Don Byron and Tony Jefferson, and sings the children's Baby Suite.

segments.title: Closing: Dat Dere
segments.summary: Asked for a closing performance, they choose Dat Dere.
